problem: The effect of the error is stated backwards. The correct energy is ∫M²/(2EI)dx. A student who writes M²/(EI) gets an energy twice as large, so ∂U/∂P and hence every deflection comes out doubled, not halved.
fix: Dropping the factor 2 in the denominator of U = ∫M²/(2EI)dx and using M²/(EI); the energy doubles, so every deflection then comes out twice as large.

problem: Squaring the moment diagram and integrating gives the strain energy, not the deflection. The sentence skips the differentiation step, which is the whole point of the chapter and of the exam trap.
fix: A Chennai workshop checking a canopy beam can square the moment diagram, integrate to get U, then differentiate with respect to the load to read the deflection.

where: Section 3, last paragraph before the summary list
problem: The symmetry of the flexibility matrix is a consequence of Maxwell/Betti, but it is not what 'makes' the unit-load equations solvable with one unknown; the single unknown comes from the single degree of indeterminacy of a propped cantilever.
fix: That symmetry halves the number of flexibility coefficients you must compute by hand, which is why the one-redundancy unit-load equation for a propped cantilever or a fixed beam is so quick to set up (see 5.8).

problem: 'a volume integral of stress times strain' omits the factor 1/2 in the strain-energy density.
fix: the moment integral becomes a volume integral of ½ × stress × strain, U = ∫ ½σε dV
